intro: This last unit brings the course together. You will read two famous passages in full. In Kiddushin 30b-32a, the rabbis ask what it means to honor and revere parents, and they learn from a jeweler in Ashkelon. In Eruvin 13b, two schools argue for three years, and a heavenly voice calls both sides the words of the living God.

Then you will do what the Talmud does. With a partner, in chavruta, you will choose a sugya, map its moves, bring in Rashi, Tosafot and a modern reader, and present both sides. Your thesis will name what the argument decides and whom the ruling protects.

By the end, you will be able to read a whole sugya, cite it by tractate and page, attribute every view to its reader and argue fairly with someone who disagrees. Those are the course's two threads, argument and mercy, in your own hands.
bigQuestion: How can a text that keeps its arguments open still guide people toward what is right and kind?

title: Great Debates and Capstone

chapters.title: Honoring Parents, and "These and Those": A Whole Sugya
chapters.bigQuestion: When two duties or two opinions pull against each other, how does the Talmud decide without silencing the losing side?

story.title: The Key Under the Pillow
story.kicker: A jeweler in Ashkelon turns down a fortune so his father can sleep, and the rabbis make him a lesson.
paragraphs: The Gemara in tractate Kiddushin, page 31a, tells of a man named Dama ben Netina. He lived in Ashkelon, a port city on the coast. He was not Jewish. He owned precious stones, and the sages came to buy one for the high priest's breastplate. The price the Gemara gives is enormous: 600,000 gold coins, and one teacher, Rav Kahana, reports 800,000.

The key to the chest was under his father's pillow. His father was asleep. Dama would not wake him, and the buyers left. The Gemara says that the next year a red heifer, a rare and needed animal, was born in his herd. When the sages came to buy it, he asked only for the sum he had lost the year before.

The story is not told for its own sake. It answers a question. Rabbi Eliezer was asked how far the duty to honor parents reaches. He answered, in the Gemara's telling, that his students should go and see what one non-Jew did in Ashkelon. A Jewish legal discussion takes its model from outside the community.

This chapter reads that page slowly, then crosses to tractate Eruvin 13b. There, two schools argue for three years, and a voice from heaven gives an answer that keeps both sides. You will map each passage move by move and ask what each argument protects.
story.think: Why might the rabbis choose a non-Jew as their model for honoring parents, rather than a famous sage?

lessons.title: Two Verses, Two Duties
lessons.mainIdea: The Gemara reads two Torah verses as two different duties: honor (kibbud) and reverence (mora).
reading: The Ten Commandments in Exodus 20:12 say to *honor* your father and mother. Leviticus 19:3 says to revere, or fear, your mother and father. The rabbis of the Talmud held that no word of the Torah is extra. So two verses with two different verbs must teach two different duties.

A *baraita*, a teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was left out of it, spells out the difference. Kiddushin 31b records it. Reverence means not standing in a parent's set place, not sitting in a parent's seat, not contradicting a parent's words and not deciding against a parent in a dispute. Honor means giving food and drink, clothing and covering, and helping a parent come in and go out.

Notice the shape. Reverence is mostly things you hold back from doing. Honor is mostly things you actively do. Later readers, like Maimonides in his code (Mishneh Torah, Laws of Rebels, chapter 6), kept this two-part structure. It gave Jewish law a practical checklist rather than a vague feeling.

words.d: kibbud in Hebrew; in the Talmud, active care for a parent such as food, clothing and help getting around
mora in Hebrew; respect shown by not doing things, such as not taking a parent's seat or contradicting them
a teaching from the rabbis of the Mishnah's era that was not included in the Mishnah

look.title: The Verse Behind the Duty
look.text: Honour thy father and thy mother, that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.
look.cite: Exodus 20:12, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: This verse names honor. Which verse does the Gemara pair it with, and what second duty does that verse add?

check.q: According to the baraita in Kiddushin 31b, which of these is an example of reverence (mora)?
choices: Not sitting in a parent's seat
check.why: The baraita lists not sitting in a parent's place as reverence; food, clothing and help getting around are honor.

check.q: Why do the rabbis read Exodus 20:12 and Leviticus 19:3 as two duties?
choices: The two verses contradict each other
They held that different words in the Torah teach different things
One verse is from the Mishnah
Leviticus was written after the Talmud
check.why: Rabbinic reading assumes no Torah word is extra, so a different verb signals a different duty.

check.q: What is a baraita?
choices: A verse from the book of Exodus
A teaching from the Mishnah's era left out of the Mishnah
check.why: A baraita is a tannaitic teaching outside the Mishnah, often quoted in the Gemara.

lessons.title: Three Partners in a Person
lessons.mainIdea: Kiddushin 30b compares honoring parents to honoring God and calls a person's parents God's partners.
reading: Kiddushin 30b sets verses side by side. Exodus 20:12 says to honor parents. Proverbs 3:9 says to honor the LORD with your wealth. A baraita notes the same verb in both and says Scripture compares the honor of parents to the honor of God. Rabbinic tradition takes this as a sign of how weighty the duty is.

The same page teaches that there are three partners in making a person: the Holy One, the father and the mother. When people honor their parents, the baraita says, God counts it as if God dwelled among them. This is *aggadah*, the Talmud's teaching through stories and sayings, placed right next to the legal rules.

The Gemara also notices order. Exodus names the father first. Leviticus names the mother first. The rabbis read this as a signal that both parents are equal in honor and reverence. A detail of word order becomes an argument about fairness inside the family.

words.d: the parts of the Talmud that teach through stories, sayings and ideas rather than legal rulings
a tractate of the Talmud; the name means 'betrothals' and it deals mostly with marriage and family duties
a rabbinic method that links two verses because they use the same word

look.title: Word Order as Evidence
look.text: Exodus 20:12: honor your father and your mother. Leviticus 19:3: revere your mother and your father. The Gemara in Kiddushin 30b-31a explains that a child might naturally honor the mother more and fear the father more, so each verse names first the parent the child might neglect.
look.prompt: Explain the rabbis' argument in your own words. What does it assume about how children treat each parent?

check.q: What two verses does Kiddushin 30b compare because they share the verb 'honor'?
check.why: The baraita links honoring parents (Exodus 20:12) with honoring the LORD with wealth (Proverbs 3:9).

check.q: What does the Gemara learn from the father being named first in one verse and the mother first in another?
choices: That both parents are equal in honor and reverence
That the father is always owed more
That the mother is always owed more
That the verses were copied wrongly
check.why: The rabbis read the reversed order as teaching that both parents are equal.

check.q: The 'three partners' teaching is an example of which part of the Talmud?
check.why: It is a saying about meaning and value, so it is aggadah, even though it sits beside legal material.

lessons.title: Whose Money Pays?
lessons.mainIdea: The Gemara asks who pays for a parent's food and clothing and records two views before it rules.
reading: The baraita says a child must feed and clothe a parent. The Gemara in Kiddushin 32a asks the practical question: from whose money? Rav Yehuda says from the child's money. Rav Natan bar Oshaya says from the parent's money. This is the classic shape of a *sugya*, a unit of Talmudic discussion built from question, proposal, proof and objection.

Each side reaches for proof. One side points to the verse comparing honor of parents to honor of God with one's wealth, which might suggest the child's own money. The other side answers from a teaching about a person's duties. After back-and-forth, the Gemara reports that the halakhah follows the view that it comes from the parent's money.

What does that ruling protect? Later codes, such as Maimonides and the Shulchan Arukh (c. 1565), add that if the parent has no money and the child does, the child must provide. The ruling guards both sides. It keeps a poor child from ruin and still keeps a needy parent from being left alone.

words.d: one unit of discussion in the Gemara, moving through questions, proofs, objections and answers
Jewish law as the rabbis develop it; also the final ruling in a particular dispute
a code of Jewish law by Rabbi Joseph Karo, printed c. 1565, still widely used

look.title: Two Amoraim Disagree
look.text: The Gemara asks: when a child feeds a parent, whose funds are used? Rav Yehuda says the child's. Rav Natan bar Oshaya says the parent's. The ruling given follows the parent's funds.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 32a, paraphrased from the Aramaic (compare the Soncino translation, 1936)
look.prompt: Which reading of the duty is more demanding for a child, and why might the Gemara still rule the other way?

check.q: In Kiddushin 32a, what question does the Gemara ask about feeding a parent?
choices: Whether it applies on the Sabbath
check.why: The Gemara asks whether the child's or the parent's funds are used.

check.q: Which view does the halakhah follow in this sugya?
choices: The child's money is always used
check.why: The Gemara rules that the cost comes from the parent's money; later codes add that a child with means provides for a parent without.

check.q: What is a sugya?
choices: One unit of Talmudic discussion with questions and answers
A single verse of the Torah
A rabbi from the Land of Israel
check.why: A sugya is a unit of Gemara discussion that moves through questions, proofs and answers.

sections.title: Stories at the Edge of Duty

lessons.title: Dama ben Netina
lessons.mainIdea: The Gemara makes a non-Jewish jeweler from Ashkelon its model of how far honoring a parent can reach.
reading: Kiddushin 31a opens the story with a question put to Rabbi Eliezer: how far does honoring parents reach? His answer is a story. Dama ben Netina of Ashkelon would not wake his sleeping father to get a key, though a huge sale was waiting. The Gemara adds that the next year a red heifer was born in his herd, and he asked only for what he had lost.

The Gemara tells a second story about Dama. His mother, in its telling, tore his silk garment and hit him in front of the city's leaders. He did not shame her in return. Rabbinic readers set the two stories together. One is about losing money. The other is about swallowing pride. Both are about restraint.

Readers have noticed the choice of hero. Rabbi Eliezer does not point to a sage or to himself. He points to someone outside the covenant community. Many modern teachers read this as the Talmud saying that goodness is visible everywhere. The Gemara itself draws a lesson for Jews: if one not commanded acts this way, how much more one who is commanded.

words.d: an ancient port city on the Mediterranean coast, south of modern Tel Aviv
a rare all-red cow the Torah (Numbers 19) requires for a purification rite
an argument from the lesser to the greater: if this is true in a light case, it is surely true in a weighty one

look.title: Go and See in Ashkelon
look.text: Rabbi Eliezer was asked how far the honor of parents goes. He said: go and see what one non-Jew in Ashkelon did, Dama ben Netina, who would not wake his father even for a great profit.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 31a, paraphrased (compare Rodkinson's abridged translation, 1896-1903, and Soncino, 1936)
look.prompt: What kind of argument does the Gemara build from this story? Name the move.

check.q: Why did Dama ben Netina refuse the sale, in the Gemara's story?
choices: He did not trust the sages
The key was under his sleeping father's pillow
check.why: Kiddushin 31a says the key lay under his father's pillow and he would not wake him.

check.q: What does the Gemara say happened the next year?
choices: A red heifer was born in his herd
check.why: The Gemara reports a red heifer was born in his herd, and he asked only for his earlier loss.

check.q: What is a kal va-chomer?
choices: A list of the Ten Commandments
An argument from a lighter case to a weightier one
check.why: Kal va-chomer reasons that what holds in a light case holds all the more in a weighty one.

lessons.title: Rabbi Tarfon's Hands
lessons.mainIdea: The rabbis praise extreme devotion to parents and still say it is only a part of what the duty asks.
reading: Kiddushin 31b tells of Rabbi Tarfon, a *tanna*, or teacher of the Mishnah's era, in the late first and early second century CE. Whenever his mother wanted to climb into bed, he bent down so she could step on him. When he praised this act in the study house, the sages told him he had not reached even half of the honor due.

Why would the rabbis answer such devotion so sharply? The Gemara's point seems to be that honor has no ceiling. It also records Rav Yosef, blind in old age, saying that when he heard his mother's footsteps he would stand up for the Divine Presence that comes near.

These stories sit beside the legal list. They do not replace it. The baraita tells what a court could expect; the stories show an ideal. Students of the page learn to ask of every story in the Gemara: is this a rule, a model or a warning? Keeping them apart helps a reader see what the page asks.

words.d: a rabbi of the Mishnah's era, up to about 200 CE; plural tannaim
a rabbi of the Gemara's era, about 200-500 CE, who explained the Mishnah; plural amoraim
in rabbinic language, the Divine Presence

look.title: Rule, Model or Warning?
look.text: Story A: Rabbi Tarfon bends so his mother can step on him to reach her bed. The sages say he has not reached half the duty. Story B: the baraita lists food, drink, clothing and help coming and going.
look.prompt: Which of these could a court enforce? Which is meant to inspire? Explain why the Gemara keeps both.

check.q: What did the sages tell Rabbi Tarfon about his devotion?
choices: He had not reached half the honor due
He had gone too far and must stop
It was forbidden to bend down
check.why: Kiddushin 31b says the sages told him he had not reached even half of the honor.

check.q: When did the tannaim teach?
check.why: Tannaim are the rabbis of the Mishnah's era, which ends around 200 CE.

check.q: What difference between the baraita's list and the Tarfon story do careful readers notice?
choices: The list is aggadah; the story is halakhah
The list is in Hebrew Bible; the story is not in the Talmud
The list states duties; the story shows an ideal
check.why: The list gives practical duties a court could expect, while the story models an ideal beyond them.

lessons.title: Where Honor Stops
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud limits the duty: a parent cannot command a child to break the Torah.
reading: Leviticus 19:3 joins two commands: revere your parents, and keep my Sabbaths. The Gemara in Bava Metzia 32a and Yevamot 5b reads the pairing as a limit. If a parent tells a child to break the Sabbath, the child does not obey, because, the Gemara reasons, both child and parent are bound to honor God.

The Gemara also shows the duty meeting real hardship. Kiddushin 31b tells of Rav Assi, whose aged mother made demands he could not meet. He left Babylonia for the Land of Israel. Maimonides later ruled that if a parent's mind is failing and a child cannot bear it, the child may arrange for others to give care.

Modern readers across Judaism use these passages in different ways. Some Orthodox teachers stress the high bar of honor. Some Conservative and Reform teachers stress the limits, especially where a parent is harmful. The Talmud gives material to both, which is part of why the page is studied so closely.

words.d: a tractate of the Talmud; the name means 'middle gate' and it deals with lost objects, loans and workers
Maimonides' code of Jewish law, completed c. 1180
a point where one duty gives way to another

look.title: Maimonides on a Failing Mind
look.text: If a parent's mind becomes confused and the child cannot endure it, the child may leave and appoint others to care for the parent properly.
look.cite: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Rebels 6:10, c. 1180, paraphrased
look.prompt: Who does this ruling protect, the parent, the child, or both? Point to words in it.

check.q: What limit does the Gemara draw from Leviticus 19:3?
choices: Reverence applies only on the Sabbath
A parent cannot command a child to break the Torah
check.why: Bava Metzia 32a and Yevamot 5b read the pairing with 'keep my Sabbaths' as a limit on obedience.

check.q: What did Rav Assi do, according to Kiddushin 31b?
choices: Left Babylonia for the Land of Israel
check.why: The Gemara says he left for the Land of Israel when he could not meet his mother's demands.

check.q: Which work contains Maimonides' ruling about a parent whose mind is failing?
check.why: The ruling is in the Mishneh Torah, Laws of Rebels 6:10.

lessons.title: Three Years of Argument
lessons.mainIdea: Eruvin 13b says a heavenly voice declared both schools' words living, yet the law follows Beit Hillel.
reading: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel were two schools of the first century CE, named for the sages Shammai and Hillel. Eruvin 13b says they argued for three years. Each said the law followed its own view. Then, the Gemara reports, a *bat kol*, a heavenly voice, came out and said: these and those are the words of the living God, and the law follows Beit Hillel.

The sentence is famous because it holds two things at once. Both positions are called words of God. Only one becomes practice. Readers have asked how both can be true. The medieval commentator Ritva, in Spain around 1300, reports a teaching that Moses was shown many ways to rule on each question, and the sages of each generation would decide.

*Eruvin* means 'mixings' or 'blendings'. The tractate deals mainly with the Sabbath enclosure that lets people carry within a shared area. That this great saying about disagreement sits in a technical tractate is typical. The Talmud's big ideas often appear in the middle of detailed law.

words.d: literally 'daughter of a voice'; in rabbinic stories, a voice from heaven
a tractate of the Talmud; the name means 'blendings' and it deals with Sabbath boundaries
the school, or house, of the sage Hillel; its rulings usually became Jewish law
the school of the sage Shammai, often stricter than Beit Hillel

look.title: The Voice in Eruvin
look.text: For three years the two schools argued. A heavenly voice came out and said: both these and those are the words of the living God, and the law follows Beit Hillel.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 13b, paraphrased (compare the Soncino translation, 1938)
look.prompt: What two claims does the voice make? Which one decides practice?

check.q: According to Eruvin 13b, what did the heavenly voice say?
choices: Beit Shammai was wrong and must stop teaching
Both schools speak the words of the living God, and the law follows Beit Hillel
The question can never be decided
check.why: The bat kol affirms both views and then rules for Beit Hillel.

check.q: What is a bat kol?
choices: A heavenly voice in rabbinic stories
check.why: Bat kol, 'daughter of a voice', names a voice from heaven in rabbinic literature.

check.q: What does the tractate Eruvin mainly deal with?
check.why: Eruvin deals with the Sabbath enclosures and boundaries that permit carrying.

lessons.title: Why Hillel Wins
lessons.mainIdea: The Gemara says Beit Hillel's law prevailed because they were kind, humble and taught the other side first.
reading: The Gemara does not leave the ruling unexplained. It asks: if both are words of the living God, why did Beit Hillel merit that the law follow them? It answers that they were gentle and patient. They studied their own words and the words of Beit Shammai. They even quoted Beit Shammai's view before their own.

Eruvin 13b gives a case. Mishnah Sukkah 2:7 records that Beit Shammai held a person whose head and most of the body were in the sukkah, but the table in the house, had not fulfilled the duty. Beit Hillel held that the person had. In the Mishnah, Beit Hillel's teaching opens by stating Beit Shammai's view first.

The Gemara ends with a moral. Whoever humbles themselves, the Holy One raises up. Whoever chases greatness, greatness runs from them. Here ARGUMENT and MERCY meet. The winner is not the stronger debater but the side that took the other side seriously.

words.d: a temporary booth Jews dwell in during the festival of Sukkot
not thinking oneself above others; the Gemara names it as Beit Hillel's quality
the first written collection of the Oral Torah, edited c. 200 CE by Rabbi Judah the Prince

look.title: Quoting Your Opponent First
look.text: Imagine two students debating a school rule. Student A states only her own view. Student B begins, 'My classmate argues this, and here is why she has a point,' then gives his view. The Gemara says the law followed the school that did what Student B does.
look.prompt: Why might quoting your opponent first make an argument more trustworthy? Use Eruvin 13b in your answer.

check.q: Why, according to Eruvin 13b, did the law follow Beit Hillel?
choices: They were gentle and taught Beit Shammai's view, even before their own
They were older than Beit Shammai
check.why: The Gemara credits Beit Hillel's patience and humility, including quoting Beit Shammai first.

check.q: Which Mishnah does the Gemara use as its example?
check.why: Eruvin 13b points to the case of the sukkah and the table in Mishnah Sukkah 2:7.

check.q: What moral does the Gemara draw at the end of this passage?
choices: Whoever humbles themselves is raised up
check.why: The Gemara concludes that God raises the humble and greatness flees those who chase it.

lessons.title: Keeping the Losing View
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah records minority opinions on purpose, so a later court may rely on them.
reading: If the law follows Beit Hillel, why record Beit Shammai at all? Mishnah Eduyot 1:5 asks this about minority views in general. It answers that they are kept so that a later court might rely on them if it sees reason. The losing view stays on the page as a possible future ruling.

Pirkei Avot 5:17 (numbered differently in some editions) adds a test. An argument for the sake of heaven will last. Its model is Hillel and Shammai. An argument not for the sake of heaven will not last. Its model is Korah and his company, who rebelled against Moses in Numbers 16.

Readers compare Eruvin 13b with Bava Metzia 59b, the oven of Akhnai. There, a heavenly voice sides with Rabbi Eliezer, and Rabbi Yehoshua answers, 'It is not in heaven' (Deuteronomy 30:12). The majority rules. Some read the two passages as in tension; others say both place the decision in human hands.

words.d: a tractate of the Mishnah; the name means 'testimonies'
a rabbinic phrase for an argument aimed at truth and good, not at winning
a view the law does not follow, which the Talmud still records

look.title: Two Heavenly Voices
look.text: Eruvin 13b: a heavenly voice rules for Beit Hillel, and the law follows it. Bava Metzia 59b: a heavenly voice sides with Rabbi Eliezer, but Rabbi Yehoshua says the Torah 'is not in heaven,' and the majority rules against Eliezer.
look.prompt: Do these passages disagree about heavenly voices? Give one reading that says yes and one that says no.

check.q: Why does Mishnah Eduyot 1:5 say minority opinions are recorded?
choices: So a later court may rely on them
check.why: Eduyot 1:5 keeps minority views so a later court could lean on them.

check.q: In Avot 5:17, which pair models an argument for the sake of heaven?
check.why: Avot names Hillel and Shammai as the model; Korah's rebellion is the opposite.

check.q: In Bava Metzia 59b, what does Rabbi Yehoshua say to the heavenly voice?
choices: These and those are the words of the living God
check.why: Quoting Deuteronomy 30:12, Rabbi Yehoshua insists the Torah's rulings are made by human judges.

lessons.title: The Moves of the Page
lessons.mainIdea: Every sugya can be mapped as a chain of moves: source, question, proof, objection, answer and ruling.
reading: Take the sugya on whose money pays for a parent's food. It starts with a source, the baraita. It asks a question: from whose funds? It gives two positions, Rav Yehuda and Rav Natan bar Oshaya. It tests each with a proof, raises an objection and answers it. It closes with a ruling. This chain is the Talmud's method.

The *Gemara* uses short Aramaic signals for each move. 'Ta shema', come and hear, brings a proof. 'Metivei', they objected, launches a challenge. 'Teyuvta', a refutation, means a view has fallen. 'Hilkheta', the law is, gives a ruling. Learning these words is like learning road signs for the page.

Mapping helps students keep track of who is speaking. The Gemara's anonymous voice, the *stam*, asks and answers much of the time. Historians such as David Weiss Halivni (1927-2022) argued that this anonymous layer was added late, after the named amoraim. Traditional readers often treat the page as one conversation.

words.d: the Aramaic discussion of the Mishnah by the amoraim; with the Mishnah it makes up the Talmud
the anonymous voice of the Gemara that asks and answers without naming a rabbi
Aramaic for 'come and hear'; it signals that a proof is being brought
Aramaic for 'a refutation'; it signals that a view has been disproved

check.q: What does the Aramaic signal 'ta shema' introduce?
check.why: 'Ta shema', come and hear, brings a proof from a source.

choices: The anonymous voice of the Gemara

lessons.title: Argument and Mercy as One Method
lessons.mainIdea: In both Kiddushin and Eruvin the argument's form serves the people the ruling protects.
reading: Look at what each passage protects. The 'whose money' ruling protects a poor child from ruin and a needy parent from neglect. The limit in Bava Metzia 32a protects a child from being ordered to do wrong. Eruvin 13b protects the losing side's dignity and its view's place on the page.

The method and the mercy are not separate. The Gemara tests every claim, so a harsh reading does not pass unchallenged. It keeps minority opinions, so a later court can show more mercy. Its heroes, Dama and Beit Hillel, win by restraint, not by force.

Readers disagree about how far to push this. Some academic readers stress that the rabbis were a small elite whose rulings reflected their own time. Many religious readers stress the text's lasting moral voice. A careful student can hold both views in the room and let the page speak.

words.d: in this course, what a ruling protects: the weak, the embarrassed, the one who might be harmed
the Talmud's way of reasoning by question, proof, objection and answer
a small group with special training or power, such as the rabbinic sages

look.title: Pages in Two Tractates

look.prompt: Kiddushin 31a sits early in an 82-folio tractate. Why might the family duties appear there rather than at the end?

choices: The dignity and record of the losing side

check.why: By affirming both views and keeping Beit Shammai on the page, the passage protects the losing side.

check.q: How do Dama and Beit Hillel both win, in the Talmud's telling?
check.why: Dama holds back from waking his father; Beit Hillel humbly teaches the other side first.

check.q: Which statement describes an academic reading rather than a religious one?

lessons.title: Two Sugyot Side by Side
lessons.mainIdea: Setting Kiddushin 31 beside Eruvin 13b shows one Talmudic habit: rules with stories, rulings with dissent.
reading: Kiddushin 30b-32a moves from verses to a baraita list, to stories of Dama, Tarfon and Assi, to a legal question about money, to limits. Eruvin 13b moves from a long dispute to a heavenly voice, to a question about why, to a Mishnah example, to a moral about humility. Both mix *halakhah* and aggadah.

Both also leave something open. Kiddushin's stories set an ideal no one fully meets. Eruvin keeps Beit Shammai's 'words of the living God' on record after the ruling. The Babylonian Talmud, completed c. 500-600 CE, rarely closes every door. Later commentators kept arguing over both pages.

When you present a sugya in the capstone, you will do what these pages do. You will state the source, trace the moves, name who is speaking and ask what is protected. You will also name what is left open and who might read it differently. That habit is the heart of this unit.

words.d: the Mishnah with the Gemara of the rabbis of Babylonia, completed c. 500-600 CE
one folio, or two-sided page, of the Talmud, such as Kiddushin 31a and 31b
a point a passage leaves unresolved for later readers

chapters.title: Capstone: Chavruta — Present a Sugya, Its Argument and Its Mercy
chapters.bigQuestion: What does it take to read a sugya with a partner, argue its sides fairly and say clearly what it protects?

story.title: Two Sides of One Page
story.kicker: Two students take opposite sides of a Talmud passage and end up agreeing on what it is about.
paragraphs: Maya and Luis stand at the front of the room with one printed page between them. It is Bava Metzia 21a-b, on lost objects, in paraphrase. Maya argues that a finder may keep scattered coins. Luis argues that the owner still has a claim. The class has a rubric and a timer.

They do not shout. Maya reads the Mishnah's line and explains the idea of an owner who has given up hope, called *yiush* in the Gemara. Luis answers with an objection the Gemara itself raises: what if the owner does not yet know the coins are gone? They trade the page back and forth, the way the rabbis traded proofs.

Near the end, Maya says something the class did not expect. She says both of them are really arguing about the same thing: how to protect a person who loses something without punishing the person who finds it. Luis nods. Their thesis is that the sugya weighs the owner's claim against the finder's honesty.

This is the capstone. You will choose a sugya, read it with a partner in *chavruta*, map its moves, bring in commentators and a modern reader, and present both sides. The goal is not to win. It is to show the argument and the mercy on the page.
story.think: Why might two students who argue opposite sides end up agreeing on what a passage is about?

lessons.title: Choosing Your Sugya
lessons.mainIdea: A good capstone sugya is short, has a clear dispute and asks what a ruling protects.
reading: This course has read many sugyot: lost objects in Bava Metzia, workers' wages, saving a life, honoring parents in Kiddushin, and 'these and those' in Eruvin 13b. Any of them can be a capstone. You may also choose another passage, as long as you can cite tractate and page and find a translation.

Choose for three things. First, length: one sugya, often half a page to a full daf. Second, a clear dispute, with named sides such as Abaye and Rava or Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. Third, stakes: a person the ruling protects, such as the worker, the finder, the owner or a person in danger.

Translations differ in status. Michael Rodkinson's Babylonian Talmud (1896-1903) is public domain but abridged and uneven, so check it against a modern edition. The Soncino (1935-52), Steinsaltz and Sefaria's William Davidson edition are not public domain; use them to read, and paraphrase them in your own words when you present.

words.d: a final project that pulls together what a course has taught
no longer under copyright, so it may be quoted and shared freely
to restate a passage in your own words while keeping its meaning

look.title: Candidate Sugyot From the Course

choices: It has a clear dispute and a person the ruling protects

check.why: The capstone asks you to map a dispute and name what it protects.

check.q: What is true of Rodkinson's translation?
choices: It is public domain but abridged and uneven

lessons.title: Reading in Chavruta
lessons.mainIdea: Chavruta is paired study in which partners read aloud, question each other and argue toward understanding.
reading: *Chavruta* comes from the Aramaic word for friend or companion. It means study in pairs. In many yeshivas and batei midrash, study halls, the room is loud with pairs reading aloud and arguing. The Talmud itself praises this. In Taanit 23a, Rava is quoted: either chavruta or death.

Taanit 7a applies Proverbs 27:17, iron sharpens iron, to students. Just as one iron blade sharpens another, the Gemara says, two scholars sharpen each other in law. Berakhot 63b warns that those who study alone grow foolish. The ideal is not a lecture but a partner.

In practice, partners take turns. One reads a line aloud and explains it. The other asks: who is speaking, what is the question, what is the proof? Then they switch. When they disagree, they return to the text. The rule of the room is to argue with ideas, never to attack the person.

words.d: study in pairs; from the Aramaic word for friend or companion
a study hall where Torah and Talmud are studied; plural batei midrash
a school devoted to traditional Jewish study, especially Talmud

look.title: Iron Sharpens Iron
look.text: Why are words of Torah compared to iron? Because as one iron sharpens another, so two scholars sharpen each other in the study of law.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 7a, on Proverbs 27:17, paraphrased (compare the Soncino translation, 1938)
look.prompt: What does the image of two blades suggest about how partners should disagree?

check.q: What does 'chavruta' mean?
choices: The anonymous voice of the Gemara
Study in pairs, from the word for companion
check.why: Chavruta, from the Aramaic for companion, is paired study.

check.q: Which verse does Taanit 7a apply to two scholars?
choices: Deuteronomy 30:12, it is not in heaven
check.why: Taanit 7a reads Proverbs 27:17 as scholars sharpening each other.

check.q: What is the main rule for disagreement in chavruta?
choices: Argue with ideas and return to the text, not attack the person
check.why: Chavruta argues over the text itself while respecting the partner.

lessons.title: Map the Moves
lessons.mainIdea: Before arguing, partners map the sugya: Mishnah, question, proof, objection, answer and ruling.
reading: Start with the *Mishnah* or baraita the sugya discusses. Write it in one sentence. Then list each move the Gemara makes. Label it: question, proof, objection, answer, story or ruling. Mark each speaker by name or as the anonymous voice. Keep the map on one sheet so both partners can see it.

Use the signal words you have learned. 'Ta shema' brings a proof. 'Metivei' raises an objection. 'Teyku', let it stand, marks a question left unresolved. 'Hilkheta' gives the ruling. When no signal appears, ask what job the line is doing. Circle each signal word you find on the page.

A map for Bava Metzia 21a might have eight to twelve moves. Do not try to capture every word. Capture the path of the argument. Your map is the backbone of your presentation, and the rubric gives it real weight. A clear map also helps your listeners follow along.

words.d: an Aramaic word closing a question the Gemara leaves unresolved
Aramaic for 'they objected'; it introduces a challenge from a source
one step in a sugya's argument, such as a question, proof or objection

look.title: Label Each Line
look.text: Line 1: The Mishnah says scattered coins belong to the finder. Line 2: Why? Because the owner has given up hope. Line 3: But he may not know he lost them yet! Line 4: A person often touches his purse, so he knows. Line 5: The law follows this.
look.prompt: Label each line as source, question, answer, objection or ruling. Which line is the key move?

check.q: What does 'teyku' signal?
check.why: Teyku closes a question the Gemara cannot settle.

check.q: What should a sugya map start with?
choices: The Mishnah or baraita the sugya discusses
check.why: The Gemara is built on a source text, so the map begins there.

check.q: What does 'metivei' introduce?
check.why: Metivei, they objected, launches a challenge.

lessons.title: Rashi at Your Elbow
lessons.mainIdea: Rashi's commentary explains the plain sense of each line and sits beside the Gemara on the printed page.
reading: Rashi, Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, lived in Troyes, France, from 1040 to 1105. His commentary on the Talmud explains words, fills in missing steps and tells the reader who is speaking. In the standard printed page, it runs in a column on the inner side, next to the binding.

Students often say they read the Gemara 'with Rashi.' When a line is unclear, Rashi supplies a short gloss. He might say what a coin was, what a verse proves or why an objection works. Many learners treat him as a patient tutor at their elbow. Each gloss is short and to the point.

For your capstone, find one place where Rashi explains a key move. Paraphrase what he says and name the line. Rashi's commentary is not a public-domain English text you can quote freely, so present it in your own words with the tractate, page and 'Rashi, s.v.' plus the word he comments on.

words.d: Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki (1040-1105) of Troyes, France, the most widely read commentator on the Talmud
a short explanation of a word or line
short for Latin 'sub verbo', 'under the word'; tells which words a commentator is explaining

look.title: Layers on the Printed Page
look.prompt: How many centuries separate the Gemara from Rashi? What problems might a reader face across that gap?

check.q: Where did Rashi live?
check.why: Rashi lived and taught in Troyes, France, 1040-1105.

check.q: What does 's.v.' tell a reader in a citation to Rashi?
check.why: S.v., 'under the word', names the phrase in the text that the comment begins with.

check.q: Where does Rashi's commentary sit on the standard printed page?
choices: Only at the back of the volume
On the inner side, near the binding
check.why: In the standard layout, Rashi runs beside the Gemara toward the binding.

lessons.title: Tosafot Push Back
lessons.mainIdea: Tosafot compare passages across the Talmud and often challenge Rashi, modeling respectful disagreement.
reading: *Tosafot*, meaning 'additions', are comments by medieval scholars in France and Germany, many of them Rashi's own descendants and students. They were active from the twelfth into the fourteenth century. Their notes run on the outer side of the printed page.

Where Rashi explains one line, Tosafot often ask how this sugya fits with another page. They notice contradictions and try to resolve them. Many times they begin by quoting Rashi, then write, in effect, 'this is hard,' and give another reading. Rashi's grandson Rabbeinu Tam was one of the best known.

In your capstone, one Tosafot comment, paraphrased, can show a second reading of your sugya. It shows that disagreement continued long after the Gemara was complete. Like Beit Hillel, Tosafot usually state the view they question before offering their own.

words.d: 'additions'; medieval comments by scholars in France and Germany, printed on the outer margin
Rabbi Jacob ben Meir (c. 1100-1171), Rashi's grandson and a leading Tosafist
two statements that seem to disagree; Tosafot often try to reconcile them

look.title: Rashi and Tosafot on One Line
look.text: Imagine a line where Rashi says a rule applies only in a city. Tosafot quote Rashi, then point to another tractate where the same rule applies in a field too. They offer a different reading that fits both pages.
look.prompt: How is Tosafot's move like an objection in the Gemara? How is it also respectful of Rashi?

check.q: What does 'Tosafot' mean?
check.why: Tosafot means 'additions', comments added to the Talmud and Rashi.

check.q: What is a typical move of Tosafot?
choices: Comparing one sugya with another and resolving contradictions
check.why: Tosafot range across the Talmud to find and resolve tensions.

check.q: Who was Rabbeinu Tam?
choices: A tanna of the first century
Rashi's grandson and a leading Tosafist
check.why: Rabbi Jacob ben Meir, Rabbeinu Tam, was Rashi's grandson and a major Tosafist.

lessons.title: One Modern Reader
lessons.mainIdea: A modern reader, religious or academic, shows how the sugya is understood and used today.
reading: Your capstone also brings in one modern reader. Rabbi Adin Steinsaltz (1937-2020) translated and explained the whole Talmud in Hebrew and later English, aiming to open the page to beginners. His notes often explain history, objects and plants. Other editions and translations exist as well.

Academic readers ask different questions. David Weiss Halivni studied how the anonymous layer was built. Daniel Boyarin and others read aggadah as literature and culture. Women scholars and teachers, including those at women's batei midrash, have raised questions earlier readers left aside.

Pick one reader and say what their approach does. Does it explain the plain sense, trace history, or draw an ethical lesson? Attribute every claim: 'Steinsaltz explains…', 'Halivni argues…'. Do not present any reader's view as the only one. Let each reader speak in their own terms.

words.d: an Israeli rabbi (1937-2020) who translated and explained the whole Babylonian Talmud
study of the Talmud using history, language and manuscripts, without deciding religious questions
to name who holds a view, such as 'Rashi explains' or 'Halivni argues'

look.title: Three Readers, One Line

look.prompt: Write one sentence for each reader, attributed. Which approach fits your capstone sugya best, and why?

check.q: What did Adin Steinsaltz do?
choices: Translated and explained the whole Talmud
check.why: Steinsaltz produced a full translation and commentary to open the Talmud to beginners.

check.q: Which sentence correctly attributes a view?
choices: Halivni argues that the anonymous layer is late

check.why: Naming the scholar attributes the claim instead of stating it as settled fact.

check.q: What does an academic reading of the Talmud do?
choices: Decides which rulings readers must follow

check.why: Academic study describes and analyzes without ruling on religious truth.

lessons.title: A Thesis About Argument and Mercy
lessons.mainIdea: A strong thesis names what the argument decides and what the ruling protects, with a citation.
reading: A thesis is one or two sentences your whole presentation defends. For this capstone it has two parts. First, what the argument decides. Second, what the ruling protects. For example: 'Bava Metzia 21b decides that a finder may keep coins once the owner has given up hope, and so protects both the owner's claim and the finder's honesty.'

Cite exactly: tractate, folio and side, like Bava Metzia 21b or Mishnah Bava Metzia 2:1. Name the translation you read, such as Rodkinson (1896-1903) or the Soncino (1935-52). If you paraphrase, say so. Paraphrase any translation that is not public domain, and mark it clearly.

Keep the minority view in your thesis or right after it. The Talmud does. A thesis that ignores the losing side misses half the page. Your partner will test this when they take the other side. A fair thesis makes room for the other side from the start.

words.d: the main claim a presentation or essay argues for
the exact place a text comes from, such as tractate, folio and side
one leaf of a book with two sides; in the Talmud, side a and side b

look.title: Strong or Weak?
look.text: Thesis A: 'Kiddushin is about parents.' Thesis B: 'Kiddushin 32a decides that a parent's needs are paid from the parent's money, protecting a poor child while later codes still require a child with means to help.'
look.prompt: Which thesis is stronger? Name two things it does that the other does not.

check.q: What two parts should the capstone thesis name?
choices: The date and the author's hometown
The longest word and the shortest line
What the argument decides and what the ruling protects
The teacher's view and the class vote
check.why: The course's two threads are argument and mercy, so the thesis names both.

choices: The Talmud itself keeps minority views in view

lessons.title: Presenting With Your Partner
lessons.mainIdea: In the presentation, partners take opposite sides, then state together what the sugya is about.
reading: Each pair gets about ten minutes. One partner presents the ruling side, the other the minority or objecting side. Each reads the key line, explains its moves and cites the page. Then you switch roles for one exchange, so each partner argues both ways.

End together. State your shared thesis: what the argument decides and what it protects. Name one commentator, Rashi or Tosafot in paraphrase, and one modern reader. Close with an open question the page leaves for later readers. Keep this closing short and clear.

The rubric below shows how points are shared. Notice that the map of moves and fair treatment of both sides carry the most weight. Winning is not on the rubric. Clear, respectful argument is. Fairness to both sides is what earns the most points here.

words.d: a scoring guide that shows what a project is judged on and how much each part counts
one round in which a speaker makes a point and the partner answers
a claim both partners agree on after arguing opposite sides

choices: One partner is declared the winner

choices: The map of moves and arguing both sides fairly

choices: Because the Gemara has no sides

lessons.title: Studying a Sacred Text in a Public School
lessons.mainIdea: Studying the Talmud in a public school means describing what readers believe, not telling anyone what to believe.
reading: In Abington School District v. Schempp (1963), the U.S. Supreme Court ruled against required Bible reading as a devotional act in public schools. The same decision said that studying religion objectively, as part of a secular education, is allowed. This course follows that line.

That is why every belief in this course is attributed. 'Rabbinic tradition holds…', 'Rashi explains…', 'historians date…'. The course does not say whether the Oral Torah came from Sinai or whether any ruling binds the reader. Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and academic readers each read the page their own way.

Close your capstone with a short reflection. What did you learn about argument, about mercy and about listening to a partner? Students of many backgrounds, and of none, have found that a page about lost coins or sleeping fathers can teach how to disagree well.

words.d: not religious; a public school's program is secular even when it studies religion
done as an act of worship rather than as study
describing fairly without taking a side on religious truth

look.title: The Court on Studying Religion
look.text: The Court said that study of the Bible or of religion, when presented objectively as part of a secular program of education, is consistent with the First Amendment.

look.prompt: How does attributing every belief help a class stay on the 'study' side of this line?

choices: Objective study of religion as part of secular education
Required daily Bible reading as worship
Teachers ruling on which faith is true
Only private schools to mention religion
check.why: The Court barred devotional Bible reading but allowed objective study of religion.

lessons.title: Looking Back, Looking Ahead
lessons.mainIdea: The capstone gathers the course's threads: the page's moves, its mercy and a partner who disagrees well.
reading: Across this course you met the Mishnah (c. 200 CE), the Gemara of Babylonia (completed c. 500-600 CE), Rashi and Tosafot, codes like Maimonides and the Shulchan Arukh, and modern readers. You learned to cite a daf and to name a translation. You also practiced reading in pairs.

The Daf Yomi program, begun in 1923, has readers study one folio a day. A full cycle of about 2,711 folios takes about seven and a half years. In January 2020, tens of thousands filled MetLife Stadium in New Jersey to mark a completion, a Siyum HaShas. Readers in Chicago and around the world took part.

You do not need to finish the Talmud to use its method. Read the source. Map the moves. Hear the other side. Ask who is protected. That is the capstone, and it is also a skill you can carry into any argument. The page is waiting for the next pair of readers.

words.d: 'a page a day'; a program begun in 1923 in which readers study one folio of the Talmud daily
a celebration marking the completion of the whole Talmud
a way of working step by step; here, reading, mapping, arguing and asking what is protected

look.title: The Talmud by the Numbers
rows: Folios in the Daf Yomi cycle

choices: Studying one folio of the Talmud a day
check.why: Daf Yomi, 'a page a day', began in 1923.

check.q: About how long is one Daf Yomi cycle?
choices: About seven and a half years
check.why: About 2,711 folios at one a day takes about seven and a half years.

check.q: What is a Siyum HaShas?
choices: A celebration of finishing the whole Talmud
check.why: It marks the completion of the entire Talmud cycle.

review.why: Chavruta, from the Aramaic for companion, is paired study.

review.q: Where does Rashi's commentary appear on the printed page?
choices: On the inner side near the binding
review.why: Rashi runs on the inner side; Tosafot on the outer.

choices: Compare passages across the Talmud and question Rashi
review.why: Tosafot range across the Talmud, noticing and resolving tensions.

review.q: What should the capstone thesis name?
choices: What the argument decides and what it protects
review.why: The thesis follows the course's two threads, argument and mercy.

review.q: Which translation may be quoted exactly because it is public domain?
review.why: Rodkinson is public domain; the others must be paraphrased.

review.q: What did Abington v. Schempp (1963) distinguish?
review.why: The Court barred devotional Bible reading but allowed objective study of religion.

review.q: Which passage praises two scholars sharpening each other?
review.why: Taanit 7a applies 'iron sharpens iron' to scholars.

review.q: What does 'teyku' mark in a sugya?
review.why: Teyku closes a question the Gemara leaves standing.
